en: The Biography of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
As for the Great Master named Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, he was born into the Brahmin caste in South India.
Heavenly Wisdom was so remarkably sagacious that he required no further instruction; even while at the breast,
he heard the Brahmins reciting the four Vedas, each consisting of forty thousand verses.
The verse consists of forty-two characters;
he could recite its text from memory and grasp its meaning.
By the age of twenty, his fame spread far and wide, and he stood preeminent among all nations.
He thoroughly mastered all worldly arts and skills, including astronomy, geography,
the *tuowei* and secret prophecies, as well as various Daoist techniques;
his three close friends were likewise paragons of their time.
They deliberated together, saying, "We have exhausted all the principles of the world that can open the divine spirit and awaken one to the profound meaning.
What more do we wish for to amuse ourselves, to indulge our passions, and to satisfy our desires?"
"This is the ultimate happiness of a lifetime.
However, since these brahmins and practitioners of the Way do not possess the status of kings or dukes, by what means could they attain it?
Only through the art of invisibility can this happiness be realized."
The four men looked at one another, their minds in perfect accord;
they went together to a master of arts to seek the method for invisibility.
The master thought to himself:
"These four brahmins have enjoyed great renown throughout the world.
Now, for the sake of their arts, these lowly beings have humbled themselves and come to me.
If I were to transmit the incantations to them," [he thought].
This man’s talent and brilliance are peerless; he knows nothing other than this lowly method.
If he were to obtain it, he would depart and could never be brought back.
For now, give him the medicine so that he may use it daily without being aware of it.
"When the medicine is exhausted, they will surely come to beg for more.
You may use a stratagem to subdue them and make them your disciples.
He then gave each of them a pill of blue medicine and told them:
"In a secluded place, grind it with water and apply it to your eyelids;
then no one will be able to see your form.
When Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna ground the medicine, he smelled its fragrance.
Thus he came to know completely the names and proportions of all medicines,
without missing even a single *zi* or *zhu* in their quantity;
Nāgārjuna recognized them according to their respective potencies.
He returned and said to the master of arts, "This medicine consists of seventy ingredients;
the proportions and quantities are all exactly according to the prescription.
The physician asked, "By what means did you know this?"
He replied, "The medicine has its own inherent potency; why do you not perceive it?
The Master then sighed in admiration and submission, remarking, "For such a person as this, even to hear [of him] is difficult."
"How much more so for the study of signs!
Why should my humble art be anything to regret? Having said this, he bestowed [the teachings] upon him in their entirety.
Those four men, having attained the art of invisibility, entered the royal palace at will.
For over a hundred days, the beautiful women within the palace were all subjected to assault.
Later, when a woman in the inner palace became pregnant, she reported the matter to the king.
The King was greatly displeased,
thinking, "How can this be such an inauspicious and strange omen?
He summoned his wise ministers to deliberate upon this matter.
An elderly person remarked, "In matters such as these, there must be two possibilities:
either it is a ghost or it is sorcery.
One may take fine soil and place it within the various gates."
He ordered the officials to guard it and eliminate all practitioners of such arts.
If these were human practitioners, their footprints would naturally appear and could be cleared away with troops;
if they were ghosts, however, there would be no footprints.
"Demons can be exorcised with incantations, while humans can be slain with blades.
Let us test this according to the prescribed methods. Upon doing so, they saw the tracks of four persons.
Thereupon, they closed all the gates and stationed several hundred strong men.
He brandished his sword and struck at the air, killing three men;
however, Nāgārjuna remained with his body crouched and breath held by the side of the king’s head.
Seven feet from the king’s head was beyond the reach of the sword.
At that time, he first realized that desire is the root of suffering;
with a mind weary of desire, he gave rise to the aspiration for renunciation, thinking:
"If I am to attain liberation..."
He went to a śramaṇa to seek the way of renunciation.
Having succeeded in doing so, he entered the mountains to visit a Buddhist stūpa, where he left the household life and received the precepts.
Within ninety days, he had recited the Tripiṭaka.
Having mastered all profound meanings,
he sought further in various sutras but found no place where they were to be obtained.
In a remote and deep location within the Snowy Mountains, there was a stupa of the Buddha.
Within the stūpa there was an elderly bhikṣu who gave him Mahāyāna sūtras.
He recited, received, and took delight in them; yet, although he understood their true meaning, he had not yet attained mastery over them.
He traveled through various countries seeking further scriptures,
but though he searched throughout Jambudvīpa, he could not find them.
He completely defeated all the non-Buddhist masters and the tenets of the śramaṇas.
He immediately gave rise to a mind of arrogance and thought to himself: "In the worldly teachings, there are many paths and methods.
Although the Buddha's sutras are subtle, when one examines them through reasoning, they are not yet exhaustive."
This can be inferred from what has not yet been exhausted;
thus it is explained so as to awaken later students,
neither contradicting principle nor failing in accordance with facts.
"What fault could there be in this?
Having reflected on this matter, he immediately intended to act upon it; he established a teacher for instruction and prepared further clothing.
Now, setting aside what is distinct within the Buddha-dharma,
I intend to manifest the characteristics of omniscience through non-reliance and non-deflection.
Having chosen an auspicious day and time, I shall [proceed] together with my disciples.
Having received the new precepts and donned the new robes, he wished to practice them immediately.
He was alone in a quiet chamber with floors of crystal.
When the Bodhisattva Mahānāga saw him in such a state, he [approached].
Pitying and commiserating him, he immediately led him into the sea.
Within his palace, he opened a treasury of the seven treasures and retrieved a casket of the seven treasures,
bestowing upon Nāgārjuna various profound and vast *vaipulya* sūtras and the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma.
Nāgārjuna studied and recited [the texts] for ninety days until he had mastered a great many;
his mind penetrated deeply, and he realized the true benefit within himself.
Nāga, knowing his state of mind, asked him:
"Have you finished reading all the sutras?
He replied, "The sutras within your various cases are so numerous and immeasurable that they cannot be exhausted.
What I have read already exceeds ten times the total of those in Jambudvīpa."
The nāga said, "Just as there are all the sūtras within my palace,
such things cannot be known elsewhere.
Nāgārjuna then obtained a chestful of various sūtras.
He had deeply entered the three levels of patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and was fully endowed with them.
The dragon then escorted him back out.
At that time, the King of South India held extremely heterodox views; he served external paths (*tīrthika*) and slandered the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
In order to convert him, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna personally carried a red banner and walked before the king.
After seven years had passed, the king finally asked in wonder,
"Who is this person walking before me?"
He replied, "I am an omniscient one.
Upon hearing this, the king was greatly astonished and asked him,
"An omniscient one has not appeared for generations."
"You have said yourself what you are; how can this be verified?
He replied, "If you wish to know whether my wisdom lies in speaking, Your Majesty should question me.
The king then thought to himself, "I am the master of wisdom and a great master of debate."
To be able to yield when questioned is not yet sufficient to be called a victory;
if, on one occasion, he does not do so, it is no small matter.
If he were not questioned at all, that would constitute a single defeat; he hesitated for a long time.
Having no other choice, he questioned him:
"What is Heaven doing now?
Nāgārjuna replied, "Heaven is currently at war with the asuras."
When the king heard these words, he was like a person choking:
unable to spit it out and yet unable to swallow it down;
wishing to reject those words, yet having no means to prove them false.
Desire is the matter at hand; there is no other point to clarify.
Before he had even finished speaking, Nāgārjuna spoke again:
"This is not a hollow argument nor a discourse intended merely to seek victory."
Within a short while, Wang Xiao waited for the result to manifest.
As soon as he finished speaking, weapons such as shields, spears, halberds, and blades began to fall from the sky one after another.
Wang said, "Although shields, spears, halberds, and lances are indeed instruments of war,"
"Why must you know whether it was the gods or the asuras who were fighting?
Nāgārjuna said, "Constructing empty words is not as good as verifying them with actual facts.
Having spoken, the fingers of the asura's hands and feet, as well as his ears and nose, descended from the sky.
Furthermore, he caused the king, his ministers, the people,
and the assembly of brahmins to see the two armies arrayed against each other in the sky; thereupon,
the king prostrated himself and submitted to the transformative power of the Dharma.
In the palace hall there were ten thousand Brahmins,
all of whom had discarded their topknots and received the precepts of accomplishment.
At that time, Nāgārjuna was widely propagating the Buddha-dharma in South India.
He subdued the non-Buddhists and extensively elucidated the Mahāyāna,
composing one hundred thousand verses of *upadeśa* (expository treatises),
as well as five thousand verses of the *Buddhamārgālaṃkāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Adornment of the Buddha Path).
He composed the *Mahāmaitrī-upāya-śāstra* in fifty verses,
which caused the Mahāyāna teachings to flourish extensively throughout India.
Furthermore, he composed the *Abhayapaddhati-śāstra* in one hundred thousand verses.
From within fearlessness, he produced the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
At that time, there was a Brahmin well-versed in incantations who,
wishing to contend with Nāgārjuna for victory using his skills, informed the King of India.
"I can subdue this king of bhikṣus; let Your Majesty test me.
The King said, "You are a great fool!
This Bodhisattva’s brilliance vies with the light of the sun and moon."
"Wisdom and the noble mind shine together;
why do you not show humility and dare to fail to offer respect?
The Brahmin replied:
"O King, why do you, being a wise man, not verify this through reason?
Yet you suppress and sever everything.
Seeing that his words were so urgent, the King requested Nāgārjuna on his behalf."
Early in the morning, they were seated together in the Zhengde Hall.
When the brahmin arrived later, he immediately performed incantations before the hall,
creating a great pond— vast, long, and pure— within which stood a thousand-petaled lotus flower.
He sat upon it himself and rebuked Nāgārjuna, saying:
"You sit on the ground like no different from a beast,
yet you wish to debate with me, a pure flower-like man of great wisdom."
At that time, Nāgārjuna also used a spell to transform himself into a six-tusked white elephant;
he walked upon the water of the pond toward the flower-throne, and with his trunk, he coiled around it, pulled it up high, and hurled it to the ground.
The Brahmin, his waist wounded and utterly exhausted,
took refuge in Nāgārjuna, saying, "I have acted recklessly and brought disgrace upon my Great Master.
I pray that you will compassionately accept me and dispel my ignorance."
There was a master of the Hīnayāna who constantly harbored resentment and jealousy.
Nāgārjuna asked him, "Do you wish for me to remain long in this world?"
He replied, "In truth, I do not wish for it.
He then withdrew into a secluded room and did not emerge for several days.
His disciples broke down the door to look at him, whereupon he had already cast off his mortal coil and departed like a cicada shedding its shell.
Since his passing, more than a hundred years have elapsed;
the various kingdoms of South India have erected temples for him and venerate him as they do a Buddha.
His mother gave birth to him beneath a tree;
consequently, he was named Ajodhana.
Ajodhana is the name of a tree.

Because he perfected the Way through a dragon, he was given the title Nāgārjuna (Dragon Tree). According to the *Dharmatara-pitaka-sūtra*, he was the thirteenth patriarch and upheld the Buddha-dharma for over three hundred years.
The Biography of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna concludes.
